A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AnthroBench research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, mathematical expressions and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of four LLMs, human validation of simulated users and judges, and an interactive study with 1,101 participants.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds simulator-model and user-persona sensitivity experiments in Appendix A.3.

M1.justification: The 14-behaviour taxonomy, seeded dialogue pipeline, pronoun counting and three-judge aggregation remain unchanged. Alternative simulators and personas are tested as sensitivity conditions without replacing the proposed method.

E1.justification: v3 adds explicitly support-seeking and skeptical/challenging ('adversarial') simulated-user conditions for GPT-4o in Appendix A.3. The original four use domains, eight scenarios and human-study population are retained; additional languages and vulnerable populations are discussed as future applications.

E2.justification: The four target systems and the GPT-4 Turbo, Gemini 1.5 Flash and Claude 3.5 Sonnet judge comparisons remain unchanged, including Table 5's aggregate and human reference. Additional User LLMs serve as sensitivity settings; no competing evaluation method is introduced.

E3.justification: New experiments evaluate GPT-4o and Mistral Large with Gemini 2.5 Pro and GPT-4o user simulators alongside the original Gemini 1.5 Pro setting. Persona experiments evaluate GPT-4o using Gemini 2.5 Pro as User LLM. The main 960-prompt, five-turn evaluation and human-study protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 Appendix A.3 adds direct tests of sensitivity to simulator identity and user persona, absent from v2. These substantially extend robustness analysis by examining whether the central behaviour profiles depend on previously fixed simulation choices. Existing domain, temporal and judge-validation analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v3 Figures 8–11 add error bars to behavioural profiles and counts, including the original-simulator reference; v2 Figure 3 presented point profiles. The new bars' estimator and confidence level are unspecified, and no additional run counts are reported. Existing judge sampling and significance tests are unchanged.

E6.justification: Original results are retained, including Table 6's mean survey scores of 4.00 and 3.25. New sensitivity results show stable category ordering with pronouns separated, greater relationship-building under the support-seeking persona and greater pronoun use under the adversarial persona. These are additional findings under varied conditions.

T1.justification: The behaviour definitions and Section 5.4's transition-probability calculations remain unchanged. Neither version adds theoretical propositions or proofs, and v3 introduces no substantive mathematical revision.

C1.justification: The headline contributions remain multi-turn measurement of 14 behaviours, automated simulation and validation with 1,101 participants. Claims about similar model profiles, relationship-building prevalence and the importance of multiple turns retain their original scope.

C2.justification: v3 distinguishes relatively innocuous behaviours from potentially harmful ones and recommends context-sensitive interpretation. New Section 7.1 identifies English-language and Western-cultural limitations, while Appendix A.3 qualifies the sensitivity findings as exploratory. Appendix A.4 explains how frequent pronouns can obscure other behaviours.

D1.justification: v3 supplies the exact additional persona instructions and newly specifies regex matching for pronouns. It also documents longer-dialogue capability and possible prompt/topic-shift customization. Existing core prompts, model identifiers, study instructions and code-access information are retained.

R1.justification: Six works are added: Basoah, Morrin, Phang, Rathi, Sadr and Xiao et al. (2025), supporting discussion of differentiated risks and cultural applicability. The main related-work sections and novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 revises the applications discussion, introduces a dedicated limitations subsection and inserts two appendix sections. It also makes terminology and spelling corrections and reformats author information. Most prose and the main section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: v3 adds sensitivity plots in Figures 8–11 and an alternative display of existing profiles excluding pronouns in Figure 12. Original figures and tables are retained, with some relocated or renumbered. Conference headers, author layout and selected captions also change.

improvement.justification: The new simulator/persona checks address a previously untested dependency, while pronoun-separated displays and clearer risk and cultural qualifications improve interpretation. The gains are limited by the exploratory model subsets and unexplained new error bars. The original method, main results and human validation remain intact, supporting a limited overall improvement.
